captions.text: CostCook turns a catering order
into your shopping list, prep, and food cost.
Here's a real order.
An order comes in.
A backyard wedding, 200 guests, Aug 15.
I type in the menu, the guest count,
and what I'm charging a head. $13.
That's all CostCook needs.
Everything you'll see comes from this page.
First, the shopping list.
Every dish's ingredients, rolled up
into one list, scaled to 200.
Red onion is in the pilaf and the salad.
Here it's one line.
15.4 lb. One bag, 25 lb.
Grouped by supplier,
in packs you can actually buy.
3 cases of chicken thigh from Sysco.
5 cases of pita from the bakery.
Each stop gets its own subtotal.
And down here, the honest number.
About $900 out the door,
$785 in what the food itself costs.
The gap is pack round-up.
This list used to be my whole evening.
Now it's done before the coffee's poured.
Then the prep list.
What the line actually cooks, after trim.
You buy almost 80 lb of chicken thigh.
59.5 lb goes in the pot.
The loss is already in the math.
The marinade? Six whole batches.
Nobody's doing that arithmetic at 5 a.m.
The pack list is the van check.
Every dish, with its portion count.
Check each one off as it's loaded.
Equipment can ride along here too.
Chafers, sternos, whatever the job needs.
Nothing off-site gets forgotten.

b6.screen: recipe food cost, then event money

captions.text: Now the part that protects you.
Every dish knows its plate cost.
These skewers: $1.74 on the plate,
yield loss included.
At $5.50 they run 31.6%.
Over my 28% target, so it's flagged.
The fix: charge $6.22 or better.
Same math for the whole event.
A dime more a guest hits the target.
I used to find out after the party.
Now I see it before I quote.
That's CostCook.
The order goes in, the lists come out,
and you know your numbers.
